I am 74 years old now, and I never went to school — I don't read those books or listen to the extension people who come to the village waving their papers. I know farming from doing it with my own hands. I started when I was 54, so that's twenty years on this same little plot. It's me, my wife, and our grandson living at home. Our son drives a truck in Handan and sends a little money now and then, but I don't ask him for farm money. This land is my responsibility.

I grow cotton on my whole 2 mu because that's what this soil does best, and after twenty years I know every corner of it. I buy improved seed from the county supply store — not the expensive hybrid that Old Wang's son buys for his big plot, but good enough that the bollworm doesn't eat me alive. I learned my lesson about saving cotton seed: it grows weak and you lose half the crop. When the soil warms up in April, I pass the rotary tiller once to break the ground, then plant by hand.

For fertilizer, I spread one bag of compound fertilizer over the whole two mu before planting and work it in with the tiller. Then when the cotton starts flowering, if the plants look yellow, I topdress with a little urea — maybe half a small bag for the whole plot. I can't afford what the big farms put down. Electricity for the pump costs money, so I irrigate twice from my well: once when the flowers open, and once when the bolls are forming. If the summer rains come, I skip one and save the cash. Cotton needs spraying for bollworm and weeds, so I spray five times through the season. I buy the cheaper bottles from the village store — I don't know the chemical names, but the shopkeeper knows what I need, and I mix it myself.

I don't hire labor. My wife helps with planting and picking, and the boy carries water when he's not in school. Two mu is just enough that our old backs can manage it, though it gets harder every year. I expect about 480 kg per mu of seed cotton if the weather is decent. Last year was dry and I only got about 420, so I'm not counting on more than that. I'm not trying anything new — at my age, change is just risk I can't take. I need enough from this crop to buy our medicine and keep food on the table.
